claim: P bodies in budding yeast have liquid-like properties.
source: In this study, we analyze P bodies in budding yeast and find that they have liquid-like properties.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3, including fusion behavior, spherical morphology, and hexanediol sensitivity.

claim: Yeast stress granules adopt a different material state from P bodies, which is reminiscent of solid protein aggregates.
source: Surprisingly, yeast stress granules adopt a different material state, which is reminiscent of solid protein aggregates and controlled by protein disaggregases.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 4 and 5, showing resistance to hexanediol and co-localization with misfolded proteins.

claim: Yeast stress granules are controlled by protein disaggregases.
source: Surprisingly, yeast stress granules adopt a different material state, which is reminiscent of solid protein aggregates and controlled by protein disaggregases.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 5D-F showing that deletion of disaggregases affects stress granule dissolution.

claim: RNP granule formation does not depend on amyloid-like aggregation.
source: By using an assay to ectopically nucleate RNP granules, we further establish that RNP granule formation does not depend on amyloid-like aggregation but rather involves many promiscuous interactions.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 2 and 4 showing that P bodies and stress granules are ThT negative and do not form SDS-resistant polymers.

claim: RNP granule formation involves many promiscuous interactions.
source: By using an assay to ectopically nucleate RNP granules, we further establish that RNP granule formation does not depend on amyloid-like aggregation but rather involves many promiscuous interactions.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 6 showing that PLDs can interact promiscuously with misfolded proteins and other PLDs.

claim: Stress granules have different properties in mammalian cells, where they show liquid-like behavior.
source: Finally, we show that stress granules have different properties in mammalian cells, where they show liquid-like behavior.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 8 showing that mammalian stress granules are spherical, undergo fusion, and are sensitive to hexanediol.

claim: The material state of RNP granules is flexible.
source: Thus, we propose that the material state of RNP granules is flexible and that the solid state of yeast stress granules is an adaptation to extreme environments, made possible by the presence of a powerful disaggregation machine.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by the observation that P bodies and stress granules have different material properties in yeast, and stress granules differ between yeast and mammalian cells.

claim: The solid state of yeast stress granules is an adaptation to extreme environments.
source: Thus, we propose that the material state of RNP granules is flexible and that the solid state of yeast stress granules is an adaptation to extreme environments, made possible by the presence of a powerful disaggregation machine.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract as a proposal based on the authors' findings.

claim: The solid state of yeast stress granules is made possible by the presence of a powerful disaggregation machine.
source: Thus, we propose that the material state of RNP granules is flexible and that the solid state of yeast stress granules is an adaptation to extreme environments, made possible by the presence of a powerful disaggregation machine.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 5 showing that disaggregases are required for stress granule dissolution.

claim: The PD of Rnq1 can form two types of assemblies in yeast cells: amyloid-like aggregates and non-amyloid assemblies.
source: Thus, we conclude that Rnq1PD can form two types of assemblies in yeast cells: amyloid-like aggregates and non-amyloid assemblies.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data in Figure 1 showing different behaviors in [PIN+] and [pin-] cells.

claim: Rnq1PD forms SDS-resistant polymers in [PIN+] cells.
source: Using this technique, we found that Rnq1PD formed SDS-resistant polymers in [PIN+] cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by SDD-AGE data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Rnq1PD structures in [PIN+] cells can be stained with the amyloid-specific dye Thioflavin T (ThT).
source: The Rnq1PD structures in [PIN+] cells could also be stained with the amyloid-specific dye Thioflavin T (ThT) (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by ThT staining data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Rnq1PD expressed in [pin−] cells does not form SDS-resistant aggregates.
source: In contrast, Rnq1PD expressed in [pin−] cells did not form SDS-resistant aggregates (Figure 1B) and it could not be stained with ThT (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by SDD-AGE and ThT staining data shown in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: 1,6-hexanediol can disrupt non-amyloid Rnq1PD assemblies but not amyloid-like assemblies.
source: Hexanediol indeed triggered the dissolution of non-amyloid Rnq1PD assemblies, whereas the amyloid form remained unaffected (Figure 1D, Video 1).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 1D and Video 1.

claim: The dissolution of non-amyloid Rnq1PD assemblies by hexanediol is reversible.
source: Importantly, this process was reversible (Figure 1E, Video 2).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 1E and Video 2.

claim: Lsm4 does not become resistant to SDS in response to glucose depletion or robust heat stress.
source: As can be seen in Figure 2C, Lsm4 did not become resistant to SDS in response to glucose depletion or robust heat stress.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by SDD-AGE data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: SDS-resistant polymers are readily detected when Lsm4 is genetically driven into an amyloid conformation.
source: In contrast, SDS-resistant polymers were readily detected, when Lsm4 was genetically driven into an amyloid conformation (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by SDD-AGE data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Lsm4 in the amyloid state forms very large complexes, whereas Lsm4 complexes in stressed cells are much smaller.
source: Lsm4 in the amyloid state formed very large complexes, whereas Lsm4 complexes in stressed cells were much smaller (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The turnover of Lsm4 in P bodies is rapid and in the same range as previously reported for mammalian P-body components.
source: As can be seen in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, the turnover of Lsm4 in P bodies was rapid and in the same range as previously reported for mammalian P-body components (Andrei et al., 2005; Kedersha et al., 2005; Aizer et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, as well as citations to previous studies.

claim: The turnover rate of Lsm4 in the amyloid conformation is much slower than in P bodies.
source: However, the turnover rate of Lsm4 in the amyloid conformation was much slower (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Stress-induced Lsm4-labeled P bodies disassemble in the presence of the translation inhibitor cycloheximide.
source: Indeed, stress-induced Lsm4-labeled P bodies disassembled in the presence of the translation inhibitor cycloheximide, an inhibitor that traps RNAs on polysomes and thereby depletes P bodies of RNA substrates (Figure 2F, Video 3).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 2F and Video 3.

claim: Lsm4 in the amyloid state is unaffected by cycloheximide.
source: In contrast, Lsm4 in the amyloid state was unaffected by cycloheximide, suggesting that the formation of this structure is independent of RNA.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 2F and Video 3.

claim: Lsm4-containing P bodies are ThT negative.
source: As shown in Figure 2G, Lsm4-containing P bodies were ThT negative, whereas amyloid-like assemblies of Lsm4 were readily identified by ThT.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by ThT staining data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Amyloid-like assemblies of Lsm4 are readily identified by ThT.
source: As shown in Figure 2G, Lsm4-containing P bodies were ThT negative, whereas amyloid-like assemblies of Lsm4 were readily identified by ThT.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by ThT staining data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Other P-body proteins with PLDs, such as Edc3 and Dcp2, do not become SDS-resistant in stressed cells.
source: Moreover, other P-body proteins with PLDs, such as Edc3 and Dcp2, did not become SDS-resistant in stressed cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), suggesting that they do not enter into amyloid-like states.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by SDD-AGE data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Amyloid-like conformational conversions are not required for the formation of P bodies in yeast.
source: Thus, we conclude that amyloid-like conformational conversions are not required for the formation of P bodies in yeast.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section as a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Yeast P-bodies have a smooth spherical surface, in agreement with a liquid-droplet state.
source: Indeed, fluorescence microscopy of yeast P-bodies revealed a smooth spherical surface, in agreement with a liquid-droplet state (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: P bodies undergo frequent fusion events.
source: Moreover, P bodies underwent frequent fusion events (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: Upon fusion, P bodies rapidly relax into a spherical shape.
source: Upon fusion, the newly formed body rapidly relaxed into a spherical shape (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Fast relaxation times of P bodies indicate that their viscosity is relatively low, in agreement with a dynamic liquid-like state.
source: Such fast relaxation times indicate that the viscosity of P bodies is relatively low, in agreement with a dynamic liquid-like state.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section as an inference from the observed fast relaxation times.

claim: Hexanediol dissolves P bodies.
source: Indeed, when we added hexanediol to yeast cells, it dissolved P bodies (Figure 3C, Video 4).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3C and Video 4.

claim: The effect of hexanediol on P bodies is rapid and reversible.
source: Importantly, this effect was rapid (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and reversible, as P bodies reformed after hexanediol washout (Figure 3D, Video 5).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3D, and Video 5.

claim: Yeast P-bodies resemble liquid droplets with physicochemical properties unlike those of solid amyloid-like aggregates.
source: Thus, we conclude that yeast P-bodies resemble liquid droplets with physicochemical properties unlike those of solid amyloid-like aggregates.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section as a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Hexanediol does not affect stress granule integrity, even when applied for extended times or in the presence of digitonin.
source: Remarkably, hexanediol did not affect stress granule integrity, even when applied for extended times or in the presence of digitonin to facilitate hexanediol entry into the cells (Figure 4A, Figures 4—figure supplement 1, Video 6).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, and Video 6.

claim: Stress granules are distinct from P bodies and may have a more solid character.
source: Thus, we conclude that stress granules are distinct from P bodies and may instead have a more solid character.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section as a conclusion based on the differential response to hexanediol.

claim: Nrp1 does not become SDS-resistant in response to stress.
source: However, Nrp1 did not become SDS-resistant in response to stress (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by SDD-AGE data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Nrp1 complexes have a very different molecular size in stressed cells compared to the amyloid-like state.
source: Nrp1 complexes also had a very different molecular size in stressed cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The turnover rate of amyloid-like Nrp1 is much slower than Nrp1 in stress granules.
source: In addition, we found that the turnover rate of amyloid-like Nrp1 was much slower (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Four additional stress granule proteins with PLDs do not form amyloid-like structures in stressed cells.
source: As a next step, we investigated four additional stress granule proteins with PLDs using SDD-AGE. However, none of these proteins formed amyloid-like structures in stressed cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by SDD-AGE data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Stress-induced Nrp1 assemblies are ThT negative.
source: Furthermore, stress-induced Nrp1 assemblies were ThT negative, whereas genetically induced Nrp1 assemblies were stainable with ThT (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by ThT staining data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Genetically induced Nrp1 assemblies are stainable with ThT.
source: Furthermore, stress-induced Nrp1 assemblies were ThT negative, whereas genetically induced Nrp1 assemblies were stainable with ThT (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by ThT staining data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: In cells exposed to a robust heat shock of 46°C, stress granule proteins co-localize with luciferase or Ubc9ts in punctate structures.
source: Indeed, in cells that were exposed to a robust heat shock of 46°C, stress granule proteins co-localized with luciferase or Ubc9ts in punctate structures (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Co-localization is observed between Nrp1 and several chaperones, such as Hsp42, Ssa1, and Hsp104.
source: Co-localization was also observed between Nrp1 and several chaperones, such as Hsp42, Ssa1, and Hsp104 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Stress granule proteins and misfolded proteins are co-deposited.
source: This indicates that stress granule proteins and misfolded proteins are co-deposited, as previously suggested (Cherkasov et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by the co-localization data, as well as a citation to a previous study.

claim: Under mild heat-shock conditions (42°C), only luciferase and Ubc9ts form visible aggregates, whereas Nrp1 remains diffusely localized.
source: Indeed, under mild heat-shock conditions only luciferase and Ubc9ts formed visible aggregates, whereas the stress granule component Nrp1 remained diffusely localized (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Stress granule components behave like misfolding-prone proteins, which reversibly aggregate into stress granules when cells are exposed to robust environmental stress.
source: These findings suggest that stress granule components behave like misfolding-prone proteins, which reversibly aggregate into stress granules, when cells are exposed to robust environmental stress.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section as an inference from the experimental data.

claim: Glucose removal causes stress granule formation, accompanied by a low level of luciferase aggregation.
source: Glucose removal also caused stress granule formation, and this was accompanied by a low level of luciferase aggregation (see Video 10).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Video 10.

claim: Under glucose depletion conditions, luciferase and stress granule components coalesce into largely distinct structures.
source: However, in contrast to heat stress conditions, luciferase and stress granule components coalesced into largely distinct structures (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: Stress granule proteins aggregate under a variety of conditions, but co-aggregation with misfolded proteins is most pronounced during robust heat shock.
source: Thus, we conclude that stress granule proteins aggregate under a variety of conditions but that co-aggregation with misfolded proteins is most pronounced during robust heat shock.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section as a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Deletion of disaggregases (Hsp104, Sse1, or Sse2) leads to more pronounced stress granule assembly and a delay in stress granule disassembly.
source: Deletion of either of the disaggregases led to more pronounced stress granule assembly and a delay in stress granule disassembly (Figure 5D,E, Video 11).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figures 5D and 5E, and Video 11.

claim: Inactivation of Hsp104 has the strongest effect on stress granule disassembly.
source: However, inactivation of Hsp104 had the strongest effect.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by the data shown in Figures 5D and 5E.

claim: Stress granules are functional aggregates and the components contained in stress granules need to be reactivated by disaggregation before cells can re-enter into the cell cycle.
source: Thus, we conclude that stress granules are functional aggregates and that the components contained in stress granules need to be reactivated by disaggregation before cells can re-enter into the cell cycle.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section as a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Cell cycle-associated RNP granules in the multinuclear fungus Ashbya gossypii are functional aggregates that are remodeled by chaperones.
source: Consistent with this, a recent report showed that cell cycle-associated RNP granules in the multinuclear fungus Ashbya gossypii are functional aggregates that are remodeled by chaperones (Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation to a recent report.

claim: Chaperones (Ssa1 and Hsp104) do not associate with μNS particles.
source: However, chaperones did not associate with μNS particles (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the particles are invisible to the protein quality control system.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: μNS particles carrying mutant luciferase on the surface are recognized by chaperones.
source: We found that both types of particles were recognized by chaperones (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2), indicating that the misfolded proteins are accessible on the particle surface.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Under normal growth conditions (25˚C), Pab1 and Pub1 are not enriched on luciferase-coated μNS particles.
source: Under normal growth conditions (25˚C), the two stress granule proteins Pab1 or Pub1 were not enriched on the particle surface (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 3, upper panels).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: During a robust heat shock, Pub1 and Pab1 accumulate on μNS particles carrying misfolded proteins.
source: However, during a robust heat shock Pub1 and Pab1 accumulated on μNS particles (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 3, lower panels).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Naked μNS particles do not recruit Pab1 or Pub1.
source: Naked particles on the other hand did not recruit Pab1 or Pub1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 4), indicating that stress granule assembly was specifically triggered by the misfolded proteins.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: Interaction of Pub1 or Pab1 with luciferase is only observed under robust heat shock and not under glucose depletion conditions.
source: Furthermore, interaction of Pub1 or Pab1 with luciferase was only observed under robust heat shock and not under glucose depletion conditions (Figure 6—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5.

claim: Misfolded proteins can nucleate the formation of stress granules under severe heat stress conditions, but not under mild stress conditions or during normal growth.
source: Thus, we conclude that misfolded proteins can nucleate the formation of stress granules under severe heat stress conditions, but not under mild stress conditions or during normal growth.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section as a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Nrp1 weakly interacts with luciferase-coated μNS particles in the absence of stress.
source: As can be seen in Figure 6D, Nrp1 weakly interacted with the particles, even in the absence of stress.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: When a robust heat shock is applied, a large amount of Nrp1 accumulates on the surface of luciferase-coated μNS particles.
source: Importantly, when we subsequently applied a robust heat shock, a large amount of Nrp1 accumulated on the surface of the particle (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The interaction between Nrp1 and misfolded proteins is sufficient to ectopically induce stress granule formation.
source: This suggests that the interaction between Nrp1 and misfolded proteins is sufficient to ectopically induce stress granule formation.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section as an inference from the experimental data.

claim: A variant of Nrp1 lacking the PLD is unable to recognize luciferase-coated particles.
source: Remarkably, this variant was unable to recognize the luciferase-coated particle (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The isolated PLD of Nrp1 shows robust binding to luciferase particles.
source: In contrast, the isolated PLD showed robust binding to luciferase particles (Figure 6E), demonstrating that the PLD is sufficient for the interaction with misfolded proteins.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: PLDs can promiscuously interact with misfolded proteins, and such promiscuous interactions can nucleate the formation of stress granules under conditions of robust heat stress.
source: Thus, PLDs can promiscuously interact with misfolded proteins, and such promiscuous interactions can nucleate the formation of stress granules, in particular under conditions of robust heat stress.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section as a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Under mild stress conditions, the activity of the cellular chaperone machinery is sufficient to prevent promiscuous interactions between misfolded proteins and stress granule components.
source: We reasoned that under mild stress conditions the activity of the cellular chaperone machinery is sufficient to prevent promiscuous interactions between misfolded proteins and stress granule components.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section as a hypothesis based on the experimental observations.

claim: When Hsp104 is inhibited, a mild heat shock is sufficient to induce the co-aggregation of endogenous Nrp1 and misfolded proteins.
source: Indeed, when Hsp104 was inhibited, a mild heat shock was sufficient to induce the co-aggregation of endogenous Nrp1 and misfolded proteins (Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 6.

claim: Preconditioning prevents the co-aggregation of stress granule components and misfolded proteins.
source: Under these conditions, Pab1 and Pub1 did not co-aggregate with misfolded proteins but formed assemblies in distinct areas of the cell (Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 7).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 7.

claim: Molecular chaperones constantly work to prevent promiscuous interactions with misfolded proteins.
source: This shows that molecular chaperones constantly work to prevent promiscuous interactions with misfolded proteins and that misfolded proteins only act as scaffolds for stress granules when the capacity of the protein quality control machinery is overrun.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section as a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Misfolded proteins only act as scaffolds for stress granules when the capacity of the protein quality control machinery is overrun.
source: This shows that molecular chaperones constantly work to prevent promiscuous interactions with misfolded proteins and that misfolded proteins only act as scaffolds for stress granules when the capacity of the protein quality control machinery is overrun.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section as a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Preconditioned cells are protected from promiscuous interactions with misfolded proteins, presumably because of the up-regulation of chaperones.
source: It also suggests that preconditioned cells are protected from promiscuous interactions with misfolded proteins, presumably because of the up-regulation of chaperones.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section as an inference from the experimental data.

claim: The RBD of Nrp1 alone is sufficient for localization to stress granules.
source: As shown in Figure 6H, the RBD alone was sufficient for localization to stress granules, whereas the PLD was not.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: The PLD of Nrp1 is not sufficient for localization to stress granules.
source: As shown in Figure 6H, the RBD alone was sufficient for localization to stress granules, whereas the PLD was not.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: PLDs are dispensable for RNP granule localization.
source: This is consistent with many other studies, which reported that PLDs are dispensable for RNP granule localization (Reijns et al., 2008; Sun et al., 2011; Cai and Futcher, 2013; Grousl et al., 2013; Kruger et al., 2013; Bley et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PLDs mediate interactions that are redundant and weak and only manifest when these domains are present at high local concentrations.
source: One potential explanation for the observed dispensability of PLDs is that they mediate interactions that are redundant and weak and thus only manifest when these domains are present at high local concentrations.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section as a hypothesis to explain the experimental observations.

claim: Particle-bound Nrp1 is able to recruit additional Nrp1 molecules from the cytosol.
source: Indeed, particle-bound Nrp1 was able to recruit additional Nrp1 molecules from the cytosol, and upon heat shock (Figure 6I, bottom panel) and glucose depletion (Figure 6—figure supplement 9, bottom panel) stress granules formed on Nrp1 particles.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6I and Figure 6—figure supplement 9.

claim: Upon heat shock and glucose depletion, stress granules form on Nrp1 particles.
source: Indeed, particle-bound Nrp1 was able to recruit additional Nrp1 molecules from the cytosol, and upon heat shock (Figure 6I, bottom panel) and glucose depletion (Figure 6—figure supplement 9, bottom panel) stress granules formed on Nrp1 particles.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6I and Figure 6—figure supplement 9.

claim: Both the PLD and the RBD of Nrp1 are able to recruit full-length Nrp1.
source: Using these particles, we found that both the PLD and the RBD were able to recruit full-length Nrp1 (Figure 6J) and promoted the formation of stress granules (Figure 6—figure supplement 11 and Figure 6—figure supplement 12).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6J, Figure 6—figure supplement 11, and Figure 6—figure supplement 12.

claim: Both the PLD and the RBD of Nrp1 promote the formation of stress granules.
source: Using these particles, we found that both the PLD and the RBD were able to recruit full-length Nrp1 (Figure 6J) and promoted the formation of stress granules (Figure 6—figure supplement 11 and Figure 6—figure supplement 12).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6J, Figure 6—figure supplement 11, and Figure 6—figure supplement 12.

claim: Stress granule assembly is highly redundant and nucleation can proceed in multiple ways, through PLDs or RBDs.
source: Together, these findings indicate that stress granule assembly is highly redundant and that nucleation can proceed in multiple ways, through PLDs or RBDs.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section as a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: PLDs work synergistically with RBDs and only function when present at a high local concentration, as during RNP granule assembly.
source: Our data further suggest that PLDs work synergistically with RBDs and only function when present at a high local concentration, as during RNP granule assembly.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section as an inference from the experimental data.

claim: P bodies show only marginal co-localization with misfolded proteins in cells exposed to robust heat stress.
source: Indeed, we found that P bodies showed only marginal co-localization with misfolded proteins in cells exposed to robust heat stress (Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Co-localization of P bodies with chaperones, such as Hsp42, Ssa1 and Hsp104, is limited.
source: Co-localization with chaperones, such as Hsp42, Ssa1 and Hsp104, was also limited (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Under normal or mild stress conditions, Hsp104 deficiency does not affect P-body formation.
source: Under normal or mild stress conditions, Hsp104 deficiency did not affect P-body formation.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section based on experimental observations.

claim: Upon robust heat stress (46°C), the P-body protein Edc3 assembles into irregular aggregate-like structures in Hsp104-deficient cells.
source: However, upon robust heat stress (46°C), the P-body protein Edc3 assembled into irregular aggregate-like structures (Figure 7C), which persisted for extended times (Video 12).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7C and Video 12.

claim: Aggregate-like Edc3 structures in Hsp104-deficient cells co-localize with the stress granule marker Pub1 and misfolded proteins.
source: These aggregate-like structures co-localized with the stress granule marker Pub1 and misfolded proteins (Figure 7D), suggesting that Edc3 is mistargeted to stress granules in the absence of Hsp104.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The amount of Edc3 that co-aggregates with misfolded proteins decreases when the expression level of Hsp104 is increased.
source: We found that the amount of Edc3 that co-aggregated with misfolded proteins decreased when the expression level of Hsp104 was increased (Figure 7E, Video 13).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7E and Video 13.

claim: Maintenance of the liquid-like P-body state requires the continuous action of Hsp104 during acute stress.
source: This indicates that maintenance of the liquid-like P-body state requires the continuous action of Hsp104 during acute stress and that P-body components are mistargeted to stress granules, when the disaggregation activity is insufficient.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section as a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: P-body components are mistargeted to stress granules when the disaggregation activity is insufficient.
source: This indicates that maintenance of the liquid-like P-body state requires the continuous action of Hsp104 during acute stress and that P-body components are mistargeted to stress granules, when the disaggregation activity is insufficient.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section as a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Mammalian stress granules and P bodies have a characteristic circular shape.
source: Indeed, the stress granules and P bodies in our cell lines had a characteristic circular shape (Figure 8A), as expected for a liquid-droplet state.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Mammalian stress granules merge and form larger structures over time.
source: We also noticed that stress granules, in particular in the early stage of stress exposure, merged and formed larger structures over time (Figure 8B, Video 14), as did P bodies (Figure 8B, Video 15).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 8B and Video 14.

claim: Mammalian P bodies merge and form larger structures over time.
source: We also noticed that stress granules, in particular in the early stage of stress exposure, merged and formed larger structures over time (Figure 8B, Video 14), as did P bodies (Figure 8B, Video 15).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 8B and Video 15.

claim: Mammalian stress granules and P bodies rapidly relax into more spherical structures after fusion.
source: In both cases, the structures rapidly relaxed into more spherical structures, in agreement with a liquid-like state.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section based on the time-lapse microscopy observations.

claim: G3BP2 is redistributed rapidly within stress granules from the unbleached to the bleached area in a half-bleach experiment.
source: The analysis of such a half-bleach event showed that G3BP2 was redistributed rapidly within stress granules from the unbleached to the bleached area (because of the small size we cannot perform a similar experiment for P bodies) (Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by half-bleach data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Hexanediol triggers the disintegration of mammalian P bodies and stress granules.
source: Hexanediol triggered the disintegration of both types of compartments, whereas a control amyloid structure, Q103-GFP, was unaffected (Figure 8D).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: A control amyloid structure, Q103-GFP, is unaffected by hexanediol.
source: Hexanediol triggered the disintegration of both types of compartments, whereas a control amyloid structure, Q103-GFP, was unaffected (Figure 8D).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Mammalian P bodies and stress granules have liquid-like properties: they turn over rapidly, are spherical, and when they fuse they relax into one spherical assembly.
source: Thus, we conclude that P bodies and stress granules have liquid-like properties in mammalian cells: they turn over rapidly, are spherical, and when they fuse they relax into one spherical assembly.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section as a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Mammalian stress granules do not overlap with luciferase aggregates under conditions of arsenate stress, proteasome inhibition, or heat shock.
source: As can be seen in Figure 8E, stress granules did not overlap with luciferase aggregates, under conditions of arsenate stress, proteasome inhibition, or heat shock.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Stress granules are formed in fundamentally different ways in yeast and mammalian cells.
source: Thus, we conclude that stress granules are formed in fundamentally different ways in yeast and mammalian cells.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section as a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: P bodies are active compartments, involved in processing and degrading mRNAs.
source: Indeed, a large body of work shows that P bodies are active compartments, involved in processing and degrading mRNAs; stress granules on the other hand do not perform biochemical reactions, but store proteins and RNAs (Anderson and Kedersha, 2009; Decker and Parker, 2012).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Stress granules do not perform biochemical reactions, but store proteins and RNAs.
source: Indeed, a large body of work shows that P bodies are active compartments, involved in processing and degrading mRNAs; stress granules on the other hand do not perform biochemical reactions, but store proteins and RNAs (Anderson and Kedersha, 2009; Decker and Parker, 2012).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Yeast P-bodies are liquid-like droplets that form by demixing from the cytoplasm.
source: Based on these findings, we propose that yeast P-bodies are liquid-like droplets that form by demixing from the cytoplasm, whereas yeast stress granules form through a liquid–solid phase transition (Figure 9).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section as a proposal based on the authors' findings.

claim: Yeast stress granules form through a liquid–solid phase transition.
source: Based on these findings, we propose that yeast P-bodies are liquid-like droplets that form by demixing from the cytoplasm, whereas yeast stress granules form through a liquid–solid phase transition (Figure 9).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section as a proposal based on the authors' findings.

claim: Mammalian cells have developed other ways of controlling stress granule assembly, primarily through posttranslational modifications of stress granule proteins.
source: Indeed, studies suggest that mammalian cells have developed other ways of controlling stress granule assembly, primarily through posttranslational modifications of stress granule proteins (Anderson and Kedersha, 2009; Buchan and Parker, 2009; Kedersha et al., 2013; Wippich et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Hexanediol perturbs the weak interactions in liquid-like assemblies, leaving stronger interactions that are characteristic of more solid-like structures intact.
source: Thus, we speculate that hexanediol perturbs the weak interactions in liquid-like assemblies, leaving stronger interactions that are characteristic of more solid-like structures intact.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section as speculation based on the authors' observations.

claim: Hexanediol could be a useful tool to probe the material properties of cellular structures.
source: This suggests that hexanediol could be a useful tool to probe the material properties of cellular structures.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section as a suggestion based on the authors' findings.

claim: Stress granule proteins carry aggregation-prone domains, which act as stress sensors.
source: However, we speculate that stress granule proteins carry aggregation-prone domains, which act as stress sensors, as previously also proposed by others (Cherkasov et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section as speculation and supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Upon stress, aggregation-prone domains in stress granule proteins expose interaction sites that promote assembly into amorphous aggregates.
source: Upon stress, these domains could expose interaction sites that promote assembly into amorphous aggregates.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section as speculation.

claim: Assembly of stress granules through sensor domains is largely specific.
source: We propose that assembly through these sensor domains is largely specific, as this would provide better control over the assembly process and could facilitate dissolution in the recovery phase.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section as a proposal.

claim: Yeast stress granules are functional aggregates, which assemble through a controlled process that is driven by a range of specific and promiscuous interactions between proteins and RNAs.
source: Thus, we propose that yeast stress granules are functional aggregates, which assemble through a controlled process that is driven by a range of specific and promiscuous interactions between proteins and RNAs.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section as a proposal based on the authors' findings.

claim: PLDs can undergo conformational conversions into amyloid-like fibers in a cell-free system.
source: This was based on the observation that these domains can undergo conformational conversions into amyloid-like fibers in a cell-free system (Han et al., 2012; Kato et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Assembly of PLDs into amyloid-like structures in cell-free systems is accompanied by the formation of hydrogels.
source: Assembly into these structures was accompanied by the formation of hydrogels, and these hydrogels could reversibly interact with other prion-like proteins in a homotypic or heterotypic manner.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section based on previous studies.

claim: Hydrogels only rearrange over long timescales, and thus can hardly provide the dynamic properties that are characteristic of RNP granules in living cells.
source: The problem with this model, however, is that hydrogels only rearrange over long timescales, and thus can hardly provide the dynamic properties that are characteristic of RNP granules in living cells (Weber and Brangwynne, 2012; Malinovska et al., 2013; Bley et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Prion-like proteins promote RNP granule formation independently of amyloid-like conversions.
source: Using this assay, we find that prion-like proteins promote RNP granule formation, but independently of amyloid-like conversions.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section based on the authors' experimental findings.

claim: Above a certain critical concentration, PLDs can promote a phase transition of RNA-binding proteins into RNP granules.
source: Thus, above a certain critical concentration, PLDs can promote a phase transition of RNA-binding proteins into RNP granules.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion based on the authors' findings.

claim: RNP granule formation is a two-step process: first, RNA-binding proteins bind to RNAs through multivalent interactions via RBDs, forming complexes of RNA and protein; second, these RNP complexes condense into RNP granules driven by promiscuous interactions between PLDs and further associations between RNAs and RBDs.
source: Based on these findings, we favor the following two-step model of RNP granule formation: First, RNA-binding proteins bind to RNAs through multivalent interactions via RBDs, forming complexes of RNA and protein; these RNP complexes may already reach a relatively large size. In the second step, these RNP complexes condense into RNP granules driven by promiscuous interactions between PLDs and further associations between RNAs and RBDs.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section as a model proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: PLDs primarily assist the final coalescence step of RNP granule formation, promoting the condensation of RNPs into large compartments.
source: In this model, the PLDs primarily assist the final coalescence step, thus, promoting the condensation of RNPs into large compartments (Figure 9).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section as part of the authors' proposed model.

claim: PLDs are not essential for RNP granule formation per se but rather promote the fusion of RNP granules and their enlargement into bigger RNP compartments.
source: In agreement with this, recent findings indicate that PLDs are not essential for RNP granule formation per se but rather promote the fusion of RNP granules and their enlargement into bigger RNP compartments (Shiina and Nakayama, 2014).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: The function of PLDs may depend on their specific local environment.
source: However, the function of PLDs may also depend on their specific local environment: In P bodies, the collective properties of PLDs may be important for maintaining a dynamic, liquid-like state, whereas in solid assemblies such as stress granules, PLDs may act as molecular glue to connect RNA-binding proteins with other RNA-binding proteins or misfolded proteins.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section as speculation by the authors.

claim: PLDs may function as adaptable interaction domains, which do not undergo conversions into structurally well-defined amyloid-like states, but mediate promiscuous interactions with many binding partners in their local environment.
source: Thus, PLDs may function as adaptable interaction domains, which do not undergo conversions into structurally well-defined amyloid-like states, but mediate promiscuous interactions with many binding partners in their local environment.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section as a proposal by the authors.

claim: In heavily stressed yeast cells, the continuous action of protein disaggregases is required to keep P bodies in a liquid-like state.
source: We found that in heavily stressed yeast cells, the continuous action of protein disaggregases is required to keep P bodies in a liquid-like state.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section based on the authors' experimental findings.

claim: The molecular composition of stress granules is a function of the cellular disaggregation activity.
source: This implies that the molecular composition of stress granules is also a function of the cellular disaggregation activity and that yeast cells try to keep a fraction of the cytoplasm in a dynamic liquid-like state, presumably to maintain their viability.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section as an inference from the authors' findings.

claim: Yeast cells try to keep a fraction of the cytoplasm in a dynamic liquid-like state, presumably to maintain their viability.
source: This implies that the molecular composition of stress granules is also a function of the cellular disaggregation activity and that yeast cells try to keep a fraction of the cytoplasm in a dynamic liquid-like state, presumably to maintain their viability.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section as an inference and speculation.

claim: Hsp104 adopts an essential function in dissolving stress granules, without which yeast cells cannot dissolve stress granules.
source: We found that the two Hsp110 disaggregases Sse1 and Sse2 make a significant contribution to the cellular disaggregation activity, but that Hsp104 adopts an essential function, without which yeast cells cannot dissolve stress granules.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section based on the authors' experimental findings.

claim: Mammalian cells do not express a Hsp104 homolog in the cytosol.
source: In contrast to yeast, mammalian cells do not express a Hsp104 homolog in the cytosol.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section as established knowledge.

claim: The ability of yeast to enter into a solid stress granule state has co-evolved with Hsp104.
source: Therefore, we speculate that the ability of yeast to enter into a solid stress granule state has co-evolved with Hsp104, providing a potential explanation for why yeast and mammalian stress granules have different material properties.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section as speculation by the authors.

claim: For yeast, formation of solid stress granules is an effective way of preserving the pre-stress state of the cytosol.
source: We conjecture that for yeast, formation of solid stress granules is an effective way of preserving the pre-stress state of the cytosol and that a selected set of yeast proteins and RNAs has been modified by evolution to aggregate upon stress.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section as a conjecture by the authors.

claim: A selected set of yeast proteins and RNAs has been modified by evolution to aggregate upon stress.
source: We conjecture that for yeast, formation of solid stress granules is an effective way of preserving the pre-stress state of the cytosol and that a selected set of yeast proteins and RNAs has been modified by evolution to aggregate upon stress.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section as a conjecture by the authors.

claim: The yeast proteome has a higher overall aggregation propensity than the human proteome.
source: Consistent with this, a recent study showed that the yeast proteome has a higher overall aggregation propensity than the human proteome (Albu et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: When stress subsides, Hsp104 reactivates the proteins and RNAs preserved in solid stress granules, promoting re-entry into the cell cycle.
source: When the stress subsides, Hsp104 reactivates the proteins and RNAs preserved in solid stress granules, thus promoting re-entry into the cell cycle.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section based on the authors' findings.

claim: Controlled entry into a solid phase can provide general protection to a cell in stressful environments.
source: Future work will show whether controlled entry into a solid phase can provide general protection to a cell in stressful environments.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section as a speculation about future research directions.
